title: Grandmaster Thinking Method
subtitle: A repeatable way to choose moves with purpose
attribution: An independent Chess Tweek course inspired by GM Igor Smirnov's publicly described teaching principles. All explanations and exercises are original to Chess Tweek.

modules.title: Repeatable Move Routine
modules.description: Build one calm sequence for reading threats, finding candidates, testing replies, and checking safety.

lessons.title: Read the last move
lessons.summary: Before looking for your move, identify what changed and what the opponent threatens now.
explanation: Every position is different after the opponent moves. Start by naming the piece that moved, the lines it opened or closed, and every new attack it created.
Deal with checks and immediate tactical threats before pursuing your own plan. A threat that can be removed while gaining time is usually stronger than passive defense.
checklist: What did the opponent's move attack or uncover?
Is any piece loose, overloaded, or facing mate?
Can I answer the threat with an active move?

exercises.prompt: White is in check. Remove the checking piece immediately.
hints: Use the white king on e1.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. Checks come before every other candidate.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: The king is still in check. Resolve the check before considering another plan.
exercises.explanation: Kxe2 removes the rook and ends the immediate threat. The routine begins with checks because no unrelated move is legal.

exercises.prompt: Black's queen threatens the king from h3. Find the active answer that removes it.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. You removed the attacking queen instead of defending passively.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: The queen on h3 remains the urgent problem. Look for a direct capture.
exercises.explanation: gxh3 wins the exposed queen and removes every threat it created. First understand the threat, then look for the most active answer.

exercises.prompt: The queen attacks the knight on c3. Save the knight while attacking the queen.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The threatened knight moves with tempo against the queen.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: Look for a safe knight square that also attacks the queen on b4.
exercises.explanation: Nd5 moves the attacked knight and attacks the queen on b4. An active defense solves the opponent's threat while creating one of your own.

lessons.title: Generate serious candidates
lessons.summary: Search forcing moves first, then add active moves that improve your position or restrict the opponent.
explanation: Checks, captures, and direct threats deserve attention because they limit the opponent's replies. They are candidates, not automatic choices.
If no forcing move works, prefer a move with a clear job: activate a piece, enter the center, gain space, or reduce the opponent's activity.
checklist: List valuable or tactically safe captures.
List direct threats the opponent must answer.
Add one active improving move when forcing play is absent.

exercises.prompt: Find the queen check that reaches the back rank and leaves the king no safe square.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The forcing check decides the position immediately.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: List the queen checks before choosing a quieter move.
exercises.explanation: Qd8 is checkmate: the king's own pawns cover its lower escape squares and the queen controls the back rank.

exercises.prompt: A valuable black piece is unprotected. Take it before looking for a slower plan.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The safe capture of the queen outranks positional improvements.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: Check every safe capture. The queen on d5 is on the rook's file.
exercises.explanation: Rxd5 wins the queen. Candidate generation prevents a player from overlooking a direct tactical gain while thinking about general plans.

exercises.prompt: Find the rook move that enters the opponent's position with check.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The active rook move forces the opponent to respond.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: Look for a rook check along the open a-file.
exercises.explanation: Ra8+ uses the open file and reaches the eighth rank with tempo. Forward activity matters when it is tactically sound.

lessons.title: Test the strongest reply
lessons.summary: Do not stop when your idea looks attractive. Ask what the opponent will do against it.
explanation: Wishful thinking evaluates only your threat. Reliable calculation gives the opponent the strongest check, capture, or counter-threat after each candidate.
A move is a serious candidate only after it survives that reply. Sometimes the right move is a quiet preparation; sometimes it is a forcing move that removes the opponent's resource.
checklist: After my candidate, what is the opponent's strongest check?
Can the opponent counter-attack something more valuable?
Does my intended follow-up still work after that reply?

exercises.prompt: Qxe4 would be met by Qxe4. Keep the queen safe while increasing pressure on e4.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. You rejected a capture that failed to the opponent's best reply.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: Before taking on e4, calculate Black's queen recapture from d5.
exercises.explanation: Qe3 keeps the queen safe and continues to contest e4. A tempting capture is not a candidate once the opponent's reply refutes it.

exercises.prompt: Rxd4 would be answered by Rxd4. Attack the rook first with the pawn.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The pawn attacks the defender before you consider taking on d4.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: Calculate Black's recapture after Rxd4, then look for a move with tempo.
exercises.explanation: c4 attacks the rook on d5. Moving the defender first changes the calculation and avoids the immediate exchange that spoiled Rxd4.

exercises.prompt: Nxe4 would allow the queen to recapture. Find the forcing knight move that removes the defender.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. You removed the defender instead of entering its recapture line.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: The queen on d5 is the defender of e4. Can the knight take it first?
exercises.explanation: Nxd5 wins the queen and eliminates the recapture on e4. Calculate the opponent's resource, then look for a move that removes it.

lessons.title: Make the final safety check
lessons.summary: Before committing, verify that your chosen move does not leave a piece or square undefended.
explanation: The final check is deliberately short. Look once more at the piece you are moving, the piece or square it used to protect, and every forcing reply available afterward.
This habit catches one-move losses without restarting the whole calculation. It is a last verification step, not an invitation to search forever.
checklist: Is the moving piece safe on its destination?
What becomes loose when the piece leaves?
Did I open a line to my king or queen?
After one last scan, can I commit without hesitation?

exercises.prompt: The bishop attacks the rook. Move the rook to the safe back-rank square.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The rook leaves the bishop's diagonal safely.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: Check the bishop's diagonal from c3 before placing the rook.
exercises.explanation: Rd1 steps off the c3-d2-e1 diagonal. A final geometry check confirms that the destination is not attacked by the bishop.

exercises.prompt: The bishop attacks the rook on e2. Move the rook one square to safety.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The rook leaves the diagonal without creating a new weakness.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: Trace the bishop's diagonal through d3 and e2, then choose a square outside it.
exercises.explanation: Re3 leaves the c4-d3-e2 diagonal. The last check confirms that the rook is no longer exposed to the bishop.

exercises.prompt: The knight attacks the queen. Move the queen to the safe central square.
exercises.correctFeedback: Correct. The queen leaves every square attacked by the knight.
exercises.incorrectFeedback: List the knight's attacks from c3 before choosing the queen's destination.
exercises.explanation: Qe3 is outside the knight's attack pattern. The final safety check verifies the destination rather than assuming every queen move is safe.

modules.title: Opening Readiness
modules.description: Develop, secure the king, and finish the opening's essential jobs before launching an attack.
